target.name: ByteCodeInterpreter value-stack consumer (primary slot 7)
target.role: the first consumer of the value stack: pops the top value, adds it to the new top in place, and leaves the sum in the lower slot
target.notes: primary dispatch slot 7, entry 0x08003D3E, 20 bytes and 10 instructions. The smallest function in the image holding the value-stack pop idiom, and a leaf with no calls and no literal pool. 84 functions in the VM surface contain the idiom (111 pops total; 69 native, 15 primary), so this is one of a family, but only this one is lifted. It consumes two values and produces one, a net counter delta of -1, and the result is written to the LOWER operand slot values[count-2] while the upper slot is abandoned rather than cleared. The counter is written back BEFORE the operand reads, which the underflow proves. There is NO underflow check: a zero counter becomes 0xFFFFFFFF, the slot address becomes context-4, and the handler decrements the word immediately BELOW the context object while touching no value slot; successive underflows walk the base four bytes further down each time. That is recorded as actual behaviour and reproduced exactly, including the 32-bit address wrap the modelling depends on. The operand order values[count-2] <op> values[count-1] is not observable in this handler because addition is commutative; it is established by the sibling at primary slot 8 (0x08003D52), which shares the first eight instructions and performs `subs r1, r2, r1`. Slots 8 and 9 are NOT lifted. No opcode table is reconstructed and no opcode index is named.

boundary_evidence.method: aligned chain-walk from each entry, following local branches

functions.role: primary dispatch slot 7: binary add over the value stack

steps.step: write the decremented counter back BEFORE any value is read
scale the index by four, so the values are word sized
form the slot address as context + count*4
read values[count-1], the OLD TOP, through [slot+4]
read values[count-2], the NEW TOP, through [slot]
store the result into the LOWER slot, values[count-2]

value_stack_access.result_slot: values[count-2], the LOWER of the two operands
value_stack_access.upper_slot: abandoned above the new counter, not cleared
value_stack_access.reads_cursor_slot_evidence: the first instruction overwrites r1 before any read of it
value_stack_access.underflow_evidence: the counter is decremented with no test and no branch, so a zero counter becomes 0xFFFFFFFF and the slot address becomes context-4
value_stack_access.operand_order: values[count-2] <op> values[count-1] on the sibling evidence
value_stack_access.deeper_operand_is_first_source_evidence: in `op Rd, Rn, Rm` the first source Rn is the left operand of the arithmetic; the sibling at slot 8 renders `subs r1, r2, r1` and r2 is the register loaded from the lower slot, so the deeper value is the left operand and slot 8 computes values[count-2] - values[count-1]

verdicts_are_independent: SEMANTIC, MODERN_BUILD and ADS_MATCH answer different questions and none is evidence for another. A passing modern build says nothing about the original compiler; a passing semantic run only removes one class of error.

identity.why_not: the original translation unit was built by ARM Developer Suite 1.2 (the surviving command line names tcpp). GCC is a different compiler with a different code generator, so its output cannot establish anything about ADS 1.2.

literal_pools.interpretation: the original's literals are accounted for by the words the unit declares; the modern build pools differently, which is a structural consequence of the compiler rather than a defect in the reconstruction. It is also why a function with a literal load cannot be compared standalone.

comparison.match_claim_note: MEASUREMENT ONLY. This compares a modern GCC build against the cartridge. A modern compiler is not the original compiler, so a difference here is expected and proves nothing; an identity here would also prove nothing about ADS 1.2. ADS_MATCH stays BLOCKED.
